unit.unitOverview: You already have two ways of talking about the future: the present continuous from Unit 10 and will from Unit 13. This unit adds the third, and then does the thing no course usually does — puts all three side by side and tells you how to choose. That choice is a genuine difficulty, not a rule to memorise, and the middle card of this unit exists only to compare. It ends with a real exchange of messages arranging a meeting, because arranging is where all three forms appear within four lines of each other.

Learn the words. Twenty-nine, in five groups.

Do the Practice. Practice 2 is the whole point of the unit.

visual.lectureScript:
This unit adds one new form and then spends most of its time on something more useful: choosing between three forms you already have.
First, the new one. Going to.
The form is be, plus going to, plus the plain verb.
I am going to look for a new job. She is going to study next year. They are going to move in March.
Be changes for person, exactly as in Unit 1 — am, is, are. Going to never changes. And the verb after it is plain.
In speech going to is usually reduced to something close to gonna. You do not need to say it that way, but you absolutely need to recognise it, because you will hear it far more often than the full form.
What does going to mean? An intention. Something you have decided to do, but have not necessarily arranged.
I'm going to look for a new job. I have decided. I have not applied for anything yet.
There is a second use, and it is worth having: a prediction based on something you can see right now.
Look at those clouds — it's going to rain.
He's going to fall.
That is evidence in front of you, leading to a conclusion. Compare it with will, which is a prediction from opinion rather than evidence. It will rain tomorrow — I think so. It's going to rain — I can see the clouds.
Now the second pattern, and this is the reason this unit exists.
You now have three ways to talk about the future. Unit 10 gave you the present continuous. Unit 13 gave you will. This unit has given you going to. I am not going to teach any of them again. What I am going to do is tell you how to choose, because the choice is a real difficulty and nobody explains it clearly.
Think of it as three degrees of how fixed the thing is.
Most fixed: the present continuous. You have arranged it. There is a time, and usually another person or a booking involved. I'm meeting her at six. I'm leaving on Tuesday. The ticket is bought, the time is agreed.
Middle: going to. You have decided, but nothing is arranged. I'm going to look for a new job. There is intention, but no appointment.
Least fixed: will. You are deciding as you speak, or predicting from opinion. I'll get them. It'll probably rain.
So the order runs: arranged, intended, decided-this-second.
Here is the test that decides most cases. Ask yourself: when did I decide this?
Before now, and I arranged it with somebody — present continuous.
Before now, but nothing is arranged — going to.
Right now, as I am speaking — will.
That single question resolves the great majority of real situations.
And here is the honest part, which most courses leave out. In a lot of sentences two of these are perfectly acceptable and native speakers would use either. I'm going to leave at six and I'm leaving at six are both fine and the difference is small. You will not be misunderstood if you choose the wrong one. What you should avoid is the one clear error: using will for something already arranged. If you booked the ticket last week, I will leave on Tuesday sounds wrong in a way the others do not.
Third pattern: arranging to meet. Two structures, and both are questions that make a suggestion.
Shall we meet at six? Shall we is a suggestion that includes the person you are speaking to. It is followed by the plain verb.
How about Thursday? How about meeting at six? How about is followed by a noun or by a verb with -ing. Not a plain verb — how about meet is wrong.
That is the one grammatical thing to remember here: shall we takes a plain verb, how about takes -ing or a noun.
And there are three replies worth having, because a suggestion needs an answer that either accepts, offers an alternative, or declines.
Accepting: Yes, that suits me. That works. Perfect.
Offering an alternative: I can't do Thursday — how about Friday? Notice you give a reason-free alternative rather than an explanation. That is normal and it is not rude.
Declining: I'm afraid I can't make it. I'm afraid is the softener, and it is doing real work — without it, I can't make it sounds abrupt.
And one last thing that is worth more than any grammar in this unit: confirm. Once a time is agreed, say it back. So, Thursday at six, at the station? Arrangements fall apart on the detail nobody repeated.
Go to Patterns.

readings.title: When Did You Decide?
readings.passageScript:
Three future forms and one question that sorts most of them.
When did you decide this?
If you decided before now and arranged it with somebody else — a time agreed, a ticket bought, a room booked — use the present continuous. I'm meeting her at six.
If you decided before now but nothing is arranged, use going to. I'm going to look for a new job. The decision exists; the appointment does not.
If you are deciding at this moment, as you speak, use will. Somebody tells you the shop shuts in ten minutes and you say I'll go now. That decision did not exist a second ago.
That question resolves most real situations, and it is worth applying deliberately for a while until it becomes automatic.
Now the part most courses leave out, and it will save you a lot of anxiety.
In a great many sentences, two of these are both acceptable and a native speaker would use either without noticing. I'm going to leave at six and I'm leaving at six are both fine. The difference between them is small and nobody will misunderstand you.
So do not treat this as a rule with a single right answer in every case. Treat it as three degrees of how fixed something is, and choose the one that matches how fixed yours actually is.
There is one error worth avoiding, because it does sound wrong. Do not use will for something already arranged. If you bought the ticket last week, I will leave on Tuesday is the one choice a listener would notice, because will suggests you are deciding as you speak — and you are not.

readings.title: How to Say No to a Time
readings.passageScript:
Arranging to meet involves saying no more often than saying yes, because the first suggestion rarely suits everybody. Learners often find this the hardest part, and it is almost entirely a matter of three fixed phrases.
The softener. I'm afraid I can't make it. Without I'm afraid, the sentence is abrupt in a way that has nothing to do with your grammar. Those two words are doing the whole job.
The alternative. This is the part that matters most and the part people leave out. Do not just decline — offer another time. I can't do Thursday, but how about Friday? A refusal with an alternative is a continuation of the conversation; a refusal without one puts all the work back on the other person.
And the reason, which is optional. This surprises people. In English you generally do not need to explain why you cannot make a time, and a long explanation can sound like an apology for something that needs none. I can't do Thursday is complete. Adding because I have a meeting is fine but not required, and adding three reasons is worse than adding none.
There is one more habit worth building and it prevents more problems than everything above. Confirm the arrangement by repeating it. So, Thursday at six, at the station? Say it back with all three pieces — day, time, place.
Arrangements almost never fail because somebody forgot the whole thing. They fail because two people agreed a day and a time and each assumed a different place, and nobody said the place out loud. The repeat-back is where that gets caught, and it takes four seconds.

grammar.title: Going to: intention, and evidence
grammar.explanation: The third future form, and the one for something you have decided but not arranged. It also has a second use for predictions you can see coming.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
FORM:  am / is / are  +  going to  +  plain verb
  I am going to look for a new job.
  She is going to study next year.
  They are going to move in March.

  be changes for person. going to never does.
  The verb after it is plain.

IN SPEECH:  going to sounds close to gonna.
  You need to RECOGNISE it. You do not
  need to say it that way.

USE 1 — INTENTION
  decided, but not arranged
     I'm going to look for a new job.

USE 2 — PREDICTION FROM EVIDENCE
  something you can see right now
     Look at those clouds - it's going to rain.
     He's going to fall.

  against will:
     It will rain tomorrow.   opinion
     It's going to rain.      evidence
grammar.workedExample:
You have decided to look for a new job but you have not applied for anything.
1. Is it arranged with anybody? No. So not the present continuous.
2. Did you decide before this moment? Yes. So not will.
3. Decided but not arranged is going to.
4. Build it: I am going to look for a new job.
Now the second use. You are outside and the sky is very dark.
1. Is this a prediction? Yes.
2. Is it based on opinion, or on something in front of you? Something in front of you.
3. Evidence takes going to: It's going to rain.
If you had simply thought tomorrow would be wet, with nothing to look at, that would be will: it will rain tomorrow.
grammar.commonMistake: Dropping be — I going to look for a job. Going to always needs am, is or are in front of it, exactly like the present continuous in Unit 10. The other error is putting -ing on the second verb: I am going to looking. Only the first verb carries -ing; the one after going to is plain.
grammar.memoryTip: Decided but not arranged. Or a prediction you can see.
grammar.practice:

2. She has decided to study next year.
3. The sky is very dark. Predict.
4. He is falling off the ladder. Predict.
5. They have decided to move in March.
6. You have decided to prepare everything tonight.
grammar.answerKey:
1. I am going to look for a new job.
2. She is going to study next year.
3. It is going to rain.
4. He is going to fall.
5. They are going to move in March.
6. I am going to prepare everything tonight.
Check two things in every answer: am, is or are is present, and the verb after going to is plain — look, study, rain, fall, move, prepare, with no -ing and no to.
Numbers 3 and 4 are the evidence use. Both are predictions about something already visible, which is what makes going to right rather than will.

grammar.title: Choosing between will, going to and the present continuous
grammar.explanation: This card teaches nothing new. All three forms are already yours — the present continuous from Unit 10, will from Unit 13, going to from card 1. What is new is choosing, which is a genuine difficulty and rarely explained.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
THREE DEGREES OF HOW FIXED IT IS

  MOST FIXED   present continuous
     arranged, with a time and usually
     another person or a booking
        I'm meeting her at six.
        I'm leaving on Tuesday.

  MIDDLE       going to
     decided, but nothing arranged
        I'm going to look for a new job.

  LEAST FIXED  will
     deciding as you speak, or predicting
     from opinion
        I'll get them.
        It'll probably rain.

THE TEST — WHEN DID YOU DECIDE?
  before now, and arranged  -> I'm -ing
  before now, not arranged  -> going to
  right now, as I speak     -> will

HONEST NOTE:
  Two of these are often BOTH fine.
  I'm going to leave at six.
  I'm leaving at six.
  Nobody will misunderstand you.

THE ONE ERROR THAT SOUNDS WRONG:
  will for something already arranged
     I will leave on Tuesday
     (ticket bought last week)  -> wrong
grammar.workedExample:
You bought a train ticket last week for Tuesday. How do you say it?
1. When did you decide? Before now.
2. Is it arranged? Yes — the ticket exists and the time is fixed.
3. Arranged takes the present continuous: I'm leaving on Tuesday.
4. Check the error: would I will leave on Tuesday be wrong? Yes, because will suggests you are deciding now, and you decided a week ago.
Now a different case. You have decided to look for a new job but done nothing about it.
1. Decided before now, so not will.
2. Arranged? No. Nothing is booked and nobody else is involved.
3. Middle case: I'm going to look for a new job.
And a third. Somebody says there are no chairs. You say I'll get some — decided this second, so will.
Three situations, three answers, one question asked each time.
grammar.commonMistake: Using will for something already arranged, which is the only choice here that clearly sounds wrong. The others overlap and are forgiving. A second error, less serious, is treating this as a rule with exactly one correct answer per sentence — in many sentences two forms are equally natural, and hesitating over which is right costs more than choosing either.
grammar.memoryTip: Ask when you decided. Arranged, intended, or deciding right now.
grammar.practice:
Choose the best form and say why in three words.
1. You bought a ticket last week for Tuesday.
2. You have decided to look for a new job. Nothing arranged.
3. Somebody says there are no chairs. You offer.
4. You are meeting a friend at six. It is agreed.
5. You think it will be cold tomorrow. No evidence in front of you.
6. The sky is black right now. Predict.
grammar.answerKey:
1. I'm leaving on Tuesday. — arranged before now
2. I'm going to look for a new job. — decided, not arranged
3. I'll get some. — deciding right now
4. I'm meeting her at six. — arranged before now
5. It will be cold tomorrow. — opinion, not evidence
6. It's going to rain. — evidence in front of you
Numbers 1 and 4 are the same case: something fixed with a time and another party. Numbers 5 and 6 are the same prediction split by evidence — opinion takes will, something visible takes going to.
If you chose going to for 1, that is not a serious error and would be understood. If you chose will for 1, that is the one that sounds wrong.

grammar.title: Arranging to meet
grammar.explanation: Two ways to suggest a time, three ways to reply, and one habit that prevents most failed arrangements. The grammar is one rule; the rest is fixed phrases.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
SUGGESTING — two structures
  Shall we  + PLAIN VERB
     Shall we meet at six?
     Shall we say Thursday?

  How about + -ING or a NOUN
     How about meeting at six?
     How about Thursday?
     NOT  How about meet at six.

REPLYING — three moves
  ACCEPT
     Yes, that suits me. / That works.
  OFFER AN ALTERNATIVE
     I can't do Thursday - how about Friday?
  DECLINE
     I'm afraid I can't make it.
     ^^^^^^^^^^ the softener does the work

THE REASON IS OPTIONAL
  I can't do Thursday.  <- complete
  You do not have to explain.

THEN CONFIRM - all three pieces:
  So, Thursday at six, at the station?
         day      time      PLACE
grammar.workedExample:
Somebody suggests Thursday and you cannot do it.
1. Soften first: I'm afraid I can't do Thursday.
2. Offer an alternative immediately, because a refusal without one puts the work back on them: how about Friday morning?
3. Notice what you did not do — you did not explain why. That is complete as it stands.
Now they accept Friday at ten.
4. Confirm with all three pieces: So, Friday at ten, in Room 2?
The confirm step is where the place gets said out loud for the first time, which is why it is worth doing even when the arrangement feels settled. Day and time get repeated naturally; the place almost never does.
And note the grammar in step 2: how about Friday is a noun, so no verb is needed. If you wanted a verb it would be how about meeting on Friday, with -ing.
grammar.commonMistake: How about meet at six — how about takes -ing or a noun, never a plain verb. Shall we is the one that takes the plain verb. The other error is declining without offering an alternative, which is grammatically perfect and ends the conversation. And the third is confirming the day and time but not the place, which is how most arrangements actually fail.
grammar.memoryTip: Shall we takes a plain verb. How about takes -ing. Always confirm the place.
grammar.practice:
Write what you would say.
1. Suggest meeting at six, using shall we.
2. Suggest Thursday, using how about.
3. Suggest meeting at six, using how about.
4. Accept a suggestion.
5. You cannot do Thursday. Decline and offer Friday.
6. Confirm an arrangement for Friday at ten at the station.
grammar.answerKey:
1. Shall we meet at six?
2. How about Thursday?
3. How about meeting at six?
4. Yes, that suits me. (or: That works.)
5. I'm afraid I can't do Thursday — how about Friday?
6. So, Friday at ten, at the station?
Compare 1 and 3. Both suggest the same thing, and the verb form is different because the structure is different: shall we meet, but how about meeting.
Number 5 has both parts — the softener and the alternative. A version with only the first is complete English and poor arranging.
Number 6 names all three pieces. Check yours has the place in it.

writing.title: Writing 1 — Your next three months
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write about the next three months of your own life.
Ten to twelve sentences.
Use the present continuous at least three times for things already arranged.
Use going to at least four times for things you have decided but not arranged.
Use will at least twice for predictions.
Then underline each one and write the reason beside it in three words.
writing.modelText:
I'm starting a new shift pattern on the first of next month — that is already agreed with my supervisor.
I'm going to ask about the training course, but I have not spoken to anybody yet.
I'm meeting my sister on the fourteenth. She booked the tickets last week.
I'm going to look for somewhere cheaper to live. Nothing is arranged.
I'm going to prepare properly for the interview this time.
I think it will be difficult for the first few weeks.
I'm visiting the other site on the ninth — that is in the diary.
I'm going to start saving something every month, even a small amount.
It will probably take longer than three months.
I'm going to ask for a reference before I leave.
writing.successCriteria: At least three present continuous for arranged things, four going to for intentions, two will for predictions; each one underlined with a three-word reason; no will used for anything already arranged
writing.support: List your next three months as plain events first, then mark each one A for arranged, D for decided, or P for prediction. The letter tells you the form, and doing it this way stops you choosing by feel.
writing.extension: Find any sentence where two forms would both be acceptable. Write both versions and say what changes.

writing.title: Writing 2 — A thread that arranges one meeting
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write a message thread between three or four people arranging one meeting.
Twelve to sixteen messages, each with a time stamp and a name.
Somebody must decline the first suggestion and offer an alternative.
Somebody must join late and ask for the original day back.
At least one message must use going to for something not yet done.
The thread must end with the day, the time and the place all confirmed in one message.
writing.modelText:
MON 08:40  Amara  We need to sort the rota before Friday. Shall we meet Wednesday?
MON 08:52  Tomas  Wednesday is fine for me. What time?
MON 08:55  Amara  How about 3pm? I'm going to check whether the small room is free.
MON 09:30  Leyla  I'm afraid I can't do Wednesday — I'm covering the front desk all afternoon. How about Thursday morning instead?
MON 09:41  Tomas  Thursday morning works.
MON 11:20  Amara  Thursday 10am then.
TUE 07:55  Rafi  Only just seen this — I'm on the early shift Thursday and I finish at 9. Could we do Wednesday after all?
TUE 08:10  Leyla  Wednesday still doesn't work for me, sorry.
TUE 08:22  Rafi  Fine — I'll come straight from the shift. 10am is doable.
TUE 08:30  Amara  Let's stay with Thursday 10am.
TUE 15:05  Amara  Small room is booked. Thursday, 10am, small room on the first floor. See you all there.
writing.successCriteria: One decline with an alternative offered; one late joiner asking for the original day; at least one going to for something not yet done; a final message naming day, time and place together; time stamps and names throughout
writing.support: Write the four people's constraints on paper before you start — who cannot do what. The thread then writes itself, because a real arrangement is just constraints colliding.
writing.extension: Now delete the final message. Read the thread again and list everything a reader still would not know.

writing.title: Writing 3 — Read the thread
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Use the message thread in Reading 3. Write full-sentence answers.
1. Why does Dani write I'm going to book something rather than I'm booking something?
2. Why does Joel write I'm visiting the Eastbourne site rather than I'm going to visit it?
3. What was never confirmed until the last message?
4. Was Priya's offer resolved, and how?
5. Even after the last message, name one thing that could still go wrong, and write the message you would send.
writing.modelText:
1. Because at that point he had decided to book but had not done it. It was an intention with nothing arranged, which is exactly what going to is for. By the final message it is done, so he states it as a fact.
2. Because it is already arranged — a fixed commitment for the whole day rather than an intention he has just formed. That is why his refusal is firm and not negotiable.
3. The place. The day and time were repeated several times, but nobody mentioned a room until the very last message.
4. Yes. Dani says send your numbers over and I'll take you through it after, so Priya is not attending but her information is included.
5. Room 2 is named without a building or a floor, and nobody has said which. I would send: Just to confirm — Room 2 is the one on the first floor, next to the kitchen. See you Friday at 10.
writing.successCriteria: Five answers, each a full sentence; answers 1 and 2 explain the form by reference to how fixed the plan was; answer 3 identifies the place; answer 5 names a real remaining ambiguity and supplies a message that resolves it
writing.support: Go through the thread and mark every message that names a day, a time, or a place. You will find days and times marked many times over and the place marked once, at the end.
writing.extension: Rewrite Dani's first message so that the whole arrangement takes three messages instead of eleven. What did you have to include?

writing.title: Writing 4 — Correct the eight mistakes
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Every sentence has exactly one mistake from this unit.
Write each out correctly and say which pattern it came from.
1. I going to look for a new job.
2. I am going to looking for a new job.
3. I will leave on Tuesday. (you bought the ticket last week)
4. How about meet at six?
5. Shall we meeting at six?
6. I can't make it. (you want it to sound softer)
7. I can't do Thursday. (you have offered nothing else)
8. So, Friday at ten? (you have not said where)
writing.modelText:
1. I am going to look for a new job. (Pattern 1 — going to always needs am, is or are)
2. I am going to look for a new job. (Pattern 1 — the verb after going to is plain)
3. I am leaving on Tuesday. (Pattern 2 — already arranged, so the present continuous)
4. How about meeting at six? (Pattern 3 — how about takes -ing or a noun)
5. Shall we meet at six? (Pattern 3 — shall we takes the plain verb)
6. I'm afraid I can't make it. (Pattern 3 — the softener is what changes how it lands)
7. I can't do Thursday — how about Friday? (Pattern 3 — a refusal should offer an alternative)
8. So, Friday at ten, at the station? (Pattern 3 — confirm all three pieces)

writing.support: Numbers 4 and 5 are the same suggestion made two ways, each with the other structure's verb form. Fix them side by side and the rule is visible: shall we meet, how about meeting.
writing.extension: Numbers 6, 7 and 8 were all correct English that would still cause a problem. Write one more of each kind.

activities.instructionsAndItems:
Write the going to form.
1. I ____ (look) for a new job.
2. She ____ (study) next year.
3. They ____ (move) in March.
4. It ____ (rain) — look at those clouds.
5. He ____ (fall)!
6. We ____ (postpone) the meeting.
7. I ____ (prepare) everything tonight.
8. She ____ (visit) her sister next month.
9. I ____ (confirm) the time tomorrow.
10. They ____ (invite) everybody.
11. It ____ (be) very busy on Friday.
12. I ____ (ask) about the training course.
activities.answerSummary:
1. am going to look  2. is going to study  3. are going to move  4. is going to rain  5. is going to fall  6. are going to postpone  7. am going to prepare  8. is going to visit  9. am going to confirm  10. are going to invite  11. is going to be  12. am going to ask

activities.sourceFile: Grade 2 Unit 8; Grade 3 Unit 8; Grade 4 Unit 9
activities.title: Practice 2 — Which future?
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Choose the best form and write the reason in three words: arranged, decided not arranged, or deciding now.
1. You bought a ticket last week for Tuesday.
2. You have decided to look for a new job. Nothing arranged.
3. Somebody says there are no chairs. You offer.
4. You are meeting a friend at six. It is agreed.
5. You think it will be cold tomorrow. No evidence.
6. The sky is black right now.
7. Your interview is on Thursday at ten. It is confirmed.
8. You have decided to start saving money.
9. Somebody says the last bus has gone. You offer to drive.
10. You have booked a room for Friday.
11. You have decided to ask for a reference. You have not asked.
12. You think the meeting will be short. It is only an opinion.
activities.answerSummary:
1. I'm leaving on Tuesday. — arranged
2. I'm going to look for a new job. — decided, not arranged
3. I'll get some. — deciding now
4. I'm meeting her at six. — arranged
5. It will be cold tomorrow. — opinion, not evidence
6. It's going to rain. — evidence in front of you
7. I'm having my interview on Thursday at ten. — arranged
8. I'm going to start saving. — decided, not arranged
9. I'll drive you. — deciding now
10. I'm using the room on Friday. — arranged
11. I'm going to ask for a reference. — decided, not arranged
12. I think it will be short. — opinion
The pattern across the twelve: four arranged, four decided, two deciding now, two predictions. The reason column matters more than the form — a learner who chooses correctly but cannot say why has not got the pattern yet.
In several of these, going to would also be acceptable and nobody would misunderstand you. The one that would sound wrong is will in numbers 1, 4, 7 or 10.

activities.title: Practice 3 — Shall we, or how about?
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Complete each suggestion correctly.
1. Shall we ____ (meet) at six?
2. How about ____ (meet) at six?
3. How about ____ (Thursday)?
4. Shall we ____ (say) Thursday?
5. How about ____ (postpone) it until Friday?
6. Shall we ____ (start) at ten?
7. How about ____ (next week)?
8. Shall we ____ (ask) the others first?
activities.answerSummary:
1. meet  2. meeting  3. Thursday  4. say  5. postponing  6. start  7. next week  8. ask
The rule is visible in 1 and 2: the same suggestion, two structures, two verb forms. Shall we takes the plain verb; how about takes -ing.
Numbers 3 and 7 are nouns, which how about also accepts. Shall we never takes a bare noun — shall we Thursday is not English.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Suggest, refuse, confirm
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Write what you would say.
1. Suggest meeting at six, using shall we.
2. Suggest Thursday, using how about.
3. Suggest meeting at six, using how about.
4. Accept a suggestion.
5. You cannot do Thursday. Decline and offer Friday.
6. You need time before you agree.
7. You can probably do Thursday but you are not sure.
8. Confirm Friday at ten at the station.
activities.answerSummary:
1. Shall we meet at six?
2. How about Thursday?
3. How about meeting at six?
4. Yes, that suits me. (or: That works.)
5. I'm afraid I can't do Thursday — how about Friday?
6. Let me check my diary.
7. Maybe Thursday — I'll confirm tomorrow.
8. So, Friday at ten, at the station?
Numbers 6 and 7 are the two most useful and the two nobody practises. Both accept the conversation without committing to the arrangement, which is very often exactly the position you are in.
Number 8 names day, time and place. Check yours has the place — that is the piece that gets left out, and it is the piece that causes the problem.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Arrange something real
activities.instructionsAndItems:
This week, arrange one real thing with somebody — a meeting, a call, a visit, a coffee.
Do it in messages or in person.
Use shall we or how about to suggest.
When a time is agreed, confirm all three pieces: day, time, place.
Write three lines: what you suggested, what was agreed, and whether the place had been said before you confirmed it.
activities.answerSummary:
No key — it is your arrangement.
What most people find: the place had not been said. Day and time get negotiated explicitly because they are what people disagree about; the place is assumed by both sides and often assumed differently.
The second finding is that confirming does not feel awkward once you have done it. It reads as organised rather than as doubtful, which is the opposite of what learners expect and the reason most people stop worrying about it after one attempt.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Listen for gonna
activities.instructionsAndItems:
This week, listen for going to in real speech — in conversation, on the radio, in a film.
Write down three examples exactly as you heard them.
Note whether the speaker said going to fully or reduced it to something like gonna.
Then note, for each one, whether it was an intention or a prediction from evidence.
activities.answerSummary:
No key.
What most people find: the reduced form is far more common than the full one in ordinary speech, and it can be hard to hear as three words at all. That is why the card asks you to recognise it rather than produce it — your own pronunciation is fine either way, but you cannot understand people if the reduced form does not register.
The second finding is that the intention use is much more common than the evidence use in everyday conversation. The evidence use appears mostly when something is about to go wrong, which is memorable but not frequent.

teacherNotes.noteType: The honest note about overlap matters
teacherNotes.note: Reading 1 and card 2 both say plainly that two forms are often equally acceptable. This is deliberate. Learners taught that each sentence has exactly one correct future form hesitate visibly in speech and over-correct in writing, and the cost of that is higher than the cost of choosing the slightly less natural option. teacherNotes.noteType: Saying no is the hard part, not suggesting
teacherNotes.note: Most arranging is declining, and Reading 2 breaks it into three fixed moves — softener, alternative, optional reason. The reason being optional surprises learners from cultures where an explanation is expected, and it is stated explicitly rather than left to be inferred. Practice 4 numbers 6 and 7 cover the position learners are most often in and least able to improvise: accepting the conversation without committing to the arrangement.
